entries.prompt: Part 1 — A writer in need of a plot
entries.answer: John Hallock is a writer under pressure from his editor, Jenkins, to produce another ghost story for the magazine, since ghost stories are what readers currently want and Hallock has a reputation for writing convincing supernatural fiction. The trouble is that Hallock has no idea what to write about; he has no plot in mind at all, yet he cannot refuse, since this magazine is the only one that regularly publishes his work. Sitting alone in his study trying to force inspiration, he begins talking to himself out loud in frustration — and is startled when a voice actually answers him. Gradually, an entire figure takes shape before him: a tall, angular woman with prominent, fish-like eyes behind heavy spectacles, her hair pulled into a tight knot, who introduces herself as a ghost named Helen.
entries.notes: Sets up the premise: writer's block leading to a supernatural visitor.

entries.prompt: Part 2 — Helen explains the Writers' Inspiration Bureau and the ghosts' strike
entries.answer: Helen explains that she was once a writer herself, in her earthly life, before becoming what she now is; in the world of spirits, she and others like her formed an organisation called the "Writers' Inspiration Bureau," whose purpose is to visit struggling writers like Hallock and help shape their ideas into workable stories. However, Helen tells him about a growing problem: the ghosts have become fed up with being constantly and carelessly summoned at all hours by people playing with Ouija boards, and as a result, the ghosts of the Bureau are threatening to go on strike, refusing to help any writer, unless the practice of using Ouija boards is stopped. Helen asks Hallock to use his influence to persuade his friends and acquaintances to give up their Ouija boards, promising to help him with his story if he succeeds.
entries.notes: Introduces the Ouija-board strike as the central complication.

entries.prompt: Part 3 — The Ouija board party and Lavinia's suspicion
entries.answer: Unfortunately for Hallock, his own wife Lavinia has recently purchased an Ouija board and has organised a party specifically to use it, dragging her reluctant husband along to take part. During the session, the board repeatedly spells out the name "Helen," and other guests begin reporting that the board keeps calling for "Hallock." Miss Hinkle, one of the guests, learns from the board that Hallock is apparently a "traitor," being called for by a woman named Helen — information that immediately makes Lavinia and the other women present suspicious that Hallock is secretly involved with another woman. Hallock, who cannot explain the situation without revealing his supernatural encounter and sounding insane, is left humiliated and unable to defend himself as his wife grows increasingly cold and accusing toward him throughout the evening.
entries.notes: Comic complication: the ghost's name creates a misunderstanding about infidelity.

entries.prompt: Part 4 — Resolution and the completed story
entries.answer: The next morning, Hallock finds his wife gone and a note slipped under his door: Lavinia has left him, declaring she is returning to her grandmother's house and that her lawyer will be in touch. Devastated, Hallock wishes himself dead, at which point Helen reappears and reveals that she had, in fact, been sent to ensure that Lavinia would give up the Ouija board for good — the entire misunderstanding at the party had been engineered as part of that plan. When Lavinia herself later returns and finally sees Helen standing behind her husband, Helen boldly confirms her own identity and explains the truth to Lavinia, who is left mortified at having wrongly accused her husband. With the Ouija board discarded for good and peace restored between the couple, Helen's mission is complete, and the ghosts of the Writers' Inspiration Bureau call off their strike. Hallock, meanwhile, finally has the vivid, first-hand ghost story he needed all along — the very events he has just lived through become his next assignment.
entries.notes: Ties together the strike plot and the marital misunderstanding; ironic ending.

entries.prompt: Humour through the supernatural and the everyday
entries.answer: Elsie Brown builds the story's comedy by placing a whimsical supernatural premise — a ghost organisation threatening a labour "strike" against being summoned — directly into the mundane domestic world of a writer and his wife's social gatherings. The ghost Helen behaves less like a frightening spectre and more like an exasperated professional colleague with grievances about working conditions, while the human characters react to supernatural events with very ordinary emotions like jealousy and suspicion. This blending of the fantastic and the domestic is the source of the story's light, satirical humour.

entries.prompt: Misunderstanding and miscommunication in marriage
entries.answer: The central conflict of the story's middle section arises purely from misunderstanding: Lavinia and her friends interpret the Ouija board's references to "Helen" as evidence of Hallock's infidelity, when the truth is entirely supernatural and, ultimately, innocent. Hallock's inability to explain the real situation without sounding delusional traps him in silence, allowing the misunderstanding to escalate unnecessarily. The story gently satirises how quickly trust can be shaken by circumstantial, incomplete information, and how communication breakdowns — rather than any real wrongdoing — can threaten a marriage.

entries.prompt: Satire of fads and the supernatural craze
entries.answer: The story pokes gentle fun at the real-world popularity of Ouija boards and séances as a fashionable social pastime, portraying Lavinia's enthusiasm for the board as a shallow social fad rather than genuine spiritual interest. By imagining the perspective of the "ghosts" themselves, who are simply annoyed at being disturbed for entertainment, Elsie Brown inverts the usual horror-story relationship between the living and the dead, using it to mock the casual, thoughtless way such supernatural practices were treated as parlour amusement.

entries.prompt: Creative inspiration born from lived experience
entries.answer: The story ends with a neat, ironic twist: Hallock, who spent the entire story unable to invent a ghost story, discovers that the very supernatural chaos he has just personally lived through — Helen's visit, the Ouija board party, his wife's near-departure — is itself the perfect ghost story. Elsie Brown suggests that genuine, vivid inspiration often comes not from forced invention but from real, lived (however extraordinary) experience, closing the story with a satisfying sense of narrative completeness.

entries.prompt: John Hallock
entries.answer: John Hallock is a professional writer struggling under pressure from his editor to produce a new ghost story despite having no plot in mind. He is generally passive and easily overwhelmed by the situations around him — unable to refuse Jenkins's demand, unable to explain the truth to his suspicious wife, and largely reactive to Helen's instructions throughout the story. His helplessness in the face of both the ghostly "strike" crisis and his own crumbling marriage provides much of the story's comedy, and his eventual "reward" — gaining a true story to write from his own chaotic experience — resolves his professional dilemma in an ironic, satisfying way.

entries.prompt: Helen (the ghost)
entries.answer: Helen is a ghost who appears to Hallock in his study, describing herself as a former writer now working for the "Writers' Inspiration Bureau," an organisation of spirits who help living writers develop their stories. She is depicted with a distinctive, slightly comic physical description — tall, angular, with prominent eyes behind heavy spectacles and hair in a tight knot — and speaks with businesslike, matter-of-fact authority rather than menace. Helen is ultimately revealed to be working deliberately, using the misunderstanding at the Ouija board party as a calculated strategy to force Lavinia to give up the board for good, showing her to be resourceful and purposeful rather than simply a passive supernatural visitor.

entries.prompt: Lavinia (Hallock's wife)
entries.answer: Lavinia is Hallock's wife, whose enthusiasm for her newly purchased Ouija board sets the story's central complication in motion. She organises a party specifically to use the board and drags her reluctant husband into participating. When the board repeatedly summons the name "Helen" in connection with her husband, Lavinia grows suspicious and hurt, ultimately leaving him a note announcing she is returning to her grandmother's house. Her willingness to believe the worst based on incomplete, supernatural "evidence" reflects the story's gentle satire of jealousy and miscommunication, though she is ultimately reconciled with Hallock once Helen reveals the truth directly to her.

entries.prompt: Jenkins
entries.answer: Jenkins is Hallock's editor, who demands another ghost story from him for the magazine, insisting it must be something genuinely frightening because that is what readers currently want. Jenkins believes Hallock is particularly suited to writing convincing ghost stories, ironically remarking that his ghosts feel like "live propositions." Though a relatively minor character who appears mainly at the story's opening, Jenkins's demand is the initial pressure that sets the entire plot in motion, since without it Hallock would never have been desperately seeking inspiration in the first place.

entries.prompt: What does the story teach about jumping to conclusions based on incomplete information?
entries.answer: The story shows how quickly trust and harmony can be disrupted when people act on partial or misleading evidence rather than seeking the full truth. Evidence: Lavinia and her friends immediately assume Hallock's infidelity purely because the Ouija board repeats the name "Helen," without any other supporting evidence, nearly ending the marriage over a misunderstanding. The lesson is to seek clarity and communication before allowing suspicion to escalate into serious consequences.

entries.prompt: What does the story suggest about respecting others' boundaries and requests, even in unfamiliar or unconventional circumstances?
entries.answer: The ghosts' grievance in the story — being disturbed constantly and carelessly by Ouija board users without regard for their own "wishes" — is treated humorously but carries a real point about respecting the boundaries of others, even when their perspective is unfamiliar or their objections seem strange. Evidence: the ghosts organise a strike specifically because their repeated pleas to stop being casually summoned go unheeded until direct, decisive action is taken. The lesson, gently delivered through comedy, is that persistent disregard for others' expressed discomfort eventually provokes real consequences.

entries.prompt: Why was John Hallock under pressure at the beginning of the story?
entries.answer: His editor, Jenkins, demanded a new ghost story for the magazine, but Hallock had no plot in mind and could not think of anything to write.

entries.prompt: How did Helen the ghost first appear to Hallock?
entries.answer: While Hallock was talking to himself aloud in frustration, a voice answered him, and gradually the figure of a tall, angular woman with prominent spectacled eyes took shape before him.

entries.prompt: What organisation did Helen say she belonged to, and what was its purpose?
entries.answer: She belonged to the "Writers' Inspiration Bureau," a group of ghosts who help writers who lack ideas by giving shape to their stories.

entries.prompt: Why were the ghosts threatening to go on strike?
entries.answer: They were tired of being constantly and carelessly summoned at all hours by people playing with Ouija boards, and wanted the practice stopped.

entries.prompt: What did Helen ask Hallock to do, and what did she promise in return?
entries.answer: She asked him to use his influence to get his friends to stop using Ouija boards, promising to help him with his ghost story if he succeeded.

entries.prompt: What happened at the Ouija board party that Lavinia organised?
entries.answer: The board repeatedly spelled out the name "Helen," and told Miss Hinkle that Hallock was a "traitor" being called for by this woman, arousing suspicion among the guests.

entries.prompt: How did Lavinia and the other women react to what the board revealed?
entries.answer: They suspected Hallock of secretly being involved with another woman named Helen, and Lavinia grew cold and accusing toward her husband.

entries.prompt: Why could Hallock not simply explain the truth to Lavinia at the party?
entries.answer: He could not explain that Helen was a ghost from the Writers' Inspiration Bureau without sounding delusional, so he remained silent and unable to defend himself.

entries.prompt: What did the note Hallock found the next morning say?
entries.answer: It said that Lavinia was leaving him to go back to her grandmother's house and that her lawyer would communicate with him.

entries.prompt: What did Helen reveal when she reappeared after Lavinia left?
entries.answer: She revealed that she had been sent to make sure Lavinia gave up the Ouija board for good, and that the misunderstanding at the party had been part of achieving that goal.

entries.prompt: How was the misunderstanding between Hallock and Lavinia finally resolved?
entries.answer: Lavinia returned, saw Helen standing behind Hallock, and Helen openly confirmed her own identity and explained the truth, clearing up the suspicion.

entries.prompt: How does the story end for Hallock as a writer?
entries.answer: Having lived through the entire strange episode with Helen and the Ouija board, Hallock finally has a vivid, genuine ghost story to write for his editor.

entries.prompt: Describe the character of Helen the ghost and explain her significance to the plot.
entries.answer:
Structured answer:

Introduction: Helen is both the story's comic supernatural centrepiece and the character whose actions ultimately resolve its central conflict.

Evidence: She appears to Hallock as a tall, angular figure with prominent spectacled eyes, explaining she belongs to the "Writers' Inspiration Bureau" and warning him of a ghosts' strike over Ouija-board misuse. Rather than being a passive visitor, she deliberately allows — or arranges — the misunderstanding at Lavinia's Ouija board party, which frightens Lavinia into abandoning the board permanently. Once this goal is achieved, Helen openly reveals herself to Lavinia and clears Hallock's name.

Conclusion: Helen functions less as a conventional horror-story ghost and more as a resourceful, purposeful problem-solver, and her actions drive both the story's comic misunderstanding and its neat resolution.

entries.prompt: Discuss how misunderstanding and miscommunication create the central conflict of the story.
entries.answer:
Structured answer:

Introduction: "A Shady Plot" derives its comic tension almost entirely from a misunderstanding rooted in incomplete information rather than any real wrongdoing.

Evidence: When the Ouija board repeatedly calls the name "Helen" in connection with Hallock, Lavinia and her friends immediately assume he is secretly involved with another woman, without seeking any other explanation. Hallock, unable to reveal the true, supernatural cause without appearing insane, remains silent, allowing suspicion to grow until Lavinia leaves him entirely.

Conclusion: The story resolves only once Helen directly clarifies the truth to Lavinia, demonstrating how easily unexamined assumptions can escalate into serious consequences, and how open communication — however strange the truth may be — is necessary to prevent lasting harm.

entries.prompt: Explain the humour in "A Shady Plot" and how Elsie Brown creates it.
entries.answer:
Structured answer:

Introduction: Elsie Brown's humour in the story comes from blending an absurd supernatural premise with recognisably human, domestic concerns.

Evidence: The idea of ghosts organising a labour "strike" over being disturbed by Ouija boards treats the supernatural with comic, bureaucratic ordinariness rather than horror. Meanwhile, the very human jealousy and suspicion that erupt at Lavinia's party — triggered by nothing more sinister than a ghost's name — show how mundane emotional reactions collide humorously with an extraordinary cause.

Conclusion: This contrast between the fantastical and the everyday, combined with the story's neat, self-referential ending in which Hallock's real-life chaos becomes his ghost story, gives "A Shady Plot" its light, satirical charm.

entries.prompt: How does the story's ending resolve both the professional and personal problems that Hallock faces?
entries.answer:
Structured answer:

Introduction: The story is carefully constructed so that its two parallel problems — Hallock's need for a ghost story and the threat to his marriage — are resolved simultaneously through the same sequence of events.

Evidence: Helen's intervention, though it temporarily worsens Hallock's domestic situation by causing Lavinia to leave, ultimately achieves its goal of ending the Ouija board practice and, once revealed, restores trust between husband and wife. At the very same time, the extraordinary, first-hand experience Hallock has lived through — a ghost, a strike, a marital crisis, and a supernatural resolution — becomes the very ghost story he had been unable to invent.

Conclusion: The story's neat double resolution reflects its central ironic idea that genuine inspiration and personal reconciliation can arise from the same unexpected, chaotic experience.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: Movement 1 — Caesar arrives, ignoring warnings
entries.answer: The excerpt opens as Julius Caesar makes his way to the Senate House on the Ides of March, passing the Soothsayer who had earlier warned him to beware this very day; Caesar dismisses the warning as coming to nothing, since the day has arrived without incident so far. Artemidorus, who has separately learned of the conspiracy against Caesar's life and prepared a letter naming the plotters, attempts to hand Caesar this letter directly and urges him to read it immediately as a matter of great personal importance, but Caesar, characteristically confident and dismissive of anything concerning himself personally, puts the matter aside and proceeds into the Senate, thereby ignoring the last direct warning that might have saved his life.
entries.notes: Draws on the immediate lead-in to the assassination itself.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: Movement 2 — The conspirators surround Caesar
entries.answer: Once inside the Senate, the conspirators put their carefully laid plan into motion. Metellus Cimber approaches Caesar with a formal petition asking that his banished brother be allowed to return to Rome, a request Caesar firmly refuses, priding himself on his own unwavering, unmovable judgement, comparing himself to the fixed North Star among the shifting stars. As Caesar refuses, the other conspirators gather closely around him, one by one adding their own pleas on Metellus's behalf, ostensibly to support the petition but in fact drawing steadily nearer to Caesar under this pretext, closing the physical distance needed for the attack about to follow. Shortly before this, Trebonius, one of the conspirators, has deliberately drawn Mark Antony aside and away from the scene, ensuring Caesar's loyal supporter cannot intervene.
entries.notes: Sets up the physical and dramatic staging of the assassination.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: Movement 3 — The stabbing and Caesar's death
entries.answer: With Caesar still refusing the petition and growing impatient with the conspirators crowding around him, Casca strikes the first blow, stabbing Caesar from behind, and the other conspirators quickly follow, each delivering their own strike in rapid succession. Caesar attempts briefly to resist and defend himself against the surrounding attackers, but upon seeing that even Brutus, whom he had trusted and loved as a close friend, is among those stabbing him, he ceases to struggle, uttering his famous, devastated exclamation of betrayal, and falls dead at the foot of Pompey's statue. The conspirators, having completed the assassination, briefly celebrate what they see as an act of liberation for Rome, with Cinna calling out that liberty and freedom have been restored.
entries.notes: The central climactic action of the excerpt.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: Movement 4 — The aftermath and Antony's uneasy alliance
entries.answer: Following the assassination, a servant of Mark Antony arrives cautiously to test the conspirators' intentions, conveying Antony's message that he wishes to know if he may safely approach and mourn Caesar, and, if so, whether he will be given a satisfactory explanation for why Caesar had to die. Brutus reassures the servant that Antony will be safe and welcomed, believing that a full explanation will satisfy him. When Antony himself arrives and speaks with apparent grief over Caesar's body, Brutus grants him permission to speak at Caesar's funeral, overriding Cassius's private warning that allowing Antony to address the Roman crowd could prove dangerous to their cause. Left alone, Antony reveals in a private aside his true feelings of grief and fury, foreshadowing the turn the public mood will take once he is given the chance to speak.
entries.notes: Sets up the dramatic irony and consequences that follow the assassination scene.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: Movement 5 — The funeral orations and the turning of the mob
entries.answer: At the Forum, Brutus first addresses the citizens of Rome, explaining that he acted for the good of Rome rather than from any personal hatred of Caesar, and the crowd, initially persuaded, begins to accept his account. Antony then steps forward to speak, and although he has agreed to say nothing against the conspirators, he masterfully turns the mood of the crowd through irony, repeatedly calling the conspirators "honourable men" while dwelling on Caesar's love for Rome, his victories and the gifts his death has robbed the people of. Reading from Caesar's will, Antony reveals that it leaves seventy-five drachmas to every Roman citizen, along with the use of his private walks, arbours and newly-planted orchards — a revelation that overwhelms the mob with grief and fury. The crowd, now inflamed, pours out of the Forum determined to burn the houses of the conspirators to the ground, and Brutus and Cassius, their position destroyed, are forced to flee the city.
entries.notes: Antony's ironic rhetoric and the will reverse public opinion against the conspirators.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: Ambition and the danger of unchecked power
entries.answer: The conspirators' central justification for killing Caesar is their fear that his growing power and popularity will lead him to become a tyrant, ending the Roman Republic's traditions of shared governance. This theme runs throughout the scene, from Caesar's own confident, almost arrogant self-description as an unmovable, superior figure among ordinary men, to the conspirators' belief that only his death can prevent unchecked ambition from destroying Roman liberty. Shakespeare presents this tension without offering an easy resolution, allowing both Caesar's genuine achievements and the conspirators' genuine fears to carry weight.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: Betrayal and the pain of broken friendship
entries.answer: The emotional core of the assassination scene lies in Caesar's discovery that Brutus, a man he trusted and loved as a friend, is among his attackers, a betrayal so devastating that it causes Caesar to stop resisting entirely and accept his death. This theme of personal betrayal, layered over the political assassination, gives the scene much of its tragic power, suggesting that the play is concerned as much with the human cost of political violence as with its constitutional justification.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: Fate, warning, and free will
entries.answer: The scene is framed by a series of ignored warnings — the Soothsayer's earlier caution to beware the Ides of March, and Artemidorus's letter naming the conspirators, both dismissed by Caesar just before his death. This pattern raises questions about fate versus free will: Caesar's death seems almost preventable, dependent on choices he actively makes to disregard clear warning signs, suggesting that his downfall stems partly from his own overconfidence rather than an unavoidable destiny.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: Political rhetoric and its consequences
entries.answer: Brutus's decision to allow Mark Antony to speak at Caesar's funeral, made against Cassius's explicit warning, plants the seed for the political consequences that follow the assassination. This choice reflects the scene's broader interest in the power of persuasive speech and public opinion in Roman politics, foreshadowing how Antony's rhetorical skill will later be used to turn the Roman crowd against the conspirators, undoing the very "liberty" they believed their action had secured.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: Julius Caesar
entries.answer: Julius Caesar appears in this scene at the height of his confidence and power, dismissing both the Soothsayer's earlier warning and Artemidorus's urgent letter as unworthy of his immediate attention. His refusal of Metellus Cimber's petition, delivered with proud, self-assured language comparing his own constancy to the fixed North Star, reveals a man convinced of his own unshakeable authority and judgement. This same confidence, however, blinds him to the danger surrounding him, and his devastated reaction upon seeing Brutus among his attackers shows that, for all his public strength, he is deeply vulnerable to personal betrayal by those he trusted.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: Brutus
entries.answer: Brutus is portrayed in this scene as a man acting, in his own mind, out of principled concern for Rome's liberty rather than personal hatred of Caesar, and his decisive participation in the stabbing — the blow that finally causes Caesar to stop resisting — reflects his belief that this act is a necessary, honourable sacrifice for the public good. His later decision to reassure Antony's servant of safety and to permit Antony to speak at the funeral, overriding Cassius's objections, further reveals his idealistic trust in fairness and open explanation, a trust that will prove strategically costly.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: Cassius
entries.answer: Cassius appears in this scene as the more politically cautious and suspicious of the conspirators, expressing clear unease at Brutus's decision to let Mark Antony speak at Caesar's funeral, correctly sensing the danger this choice poses to their cause. Though Brutus overrules him, Cassius's doubts in this scene mark him as a sharper, more pragmatic political mind than Brutus, whose idealism leads him to underestimate the risk Antony represents.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: Casca
entries.answer: Casca is the conspirator who strikes the first blow against Caesar, initiating the assassination after Caesar's impatient refusal of Metellus Cimber's petition. His willingness to act first, ahead of the other conspirators, marks him as more overtly aggressive and decisive in this scene than some of his fellow plotters, setting the assassination in motion at its critical moment.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: Mark Antony
entries.answer: Mark Antony, deliberately drawn away from Caesar's side by Trebonius just before the assassination, returns to the scene once Caesar is already dead. He cautiously tests the conspirators' intentions through his servant before approaching in person, and once granted safety and permission to speak at the funeral by Brutus, he expresses apparent grief over Caesar's body. His private aside once left alone, however, reveals genuine fury and grief beneath his outward composure, hinting at the powerful, consequential funeral oration he will go on to deliver against the conspirators.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: What does the scene teach about the danger of ignoring clear warnings out of overconfidence?
entries.answer: The scene shows how overconfidence and pride can blind a person to real danger, even when warnings are delivered clearly and directly. Evidence: Caesar dismisses both the Soothsayer's earlier caution and Artemidorus's urgent letter naming the conspirators, choosing his own self-assured judgement over these direct warnings, and is assassinated shortly after. The lesson is to remain humble and attentive to genuine warning signs, rather than assuming one's own judgement or position makes one immune to danger.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: What does the scene teach about the value of caution in political and personal judgement?
entries.answer: The scene demonstrates the risks of idealistic trust when practical caution is called for, particularly in high-stakes political situations. Evidence: Brutus's decision to reassure Antony and allow him to speak at Caesar's funeral, made against Cassius's explicit warning, sets in motion consequences that will prove costly to the conspirators. The lesson is that good intentions and trust in fairness must sometimes be balanced against careful, realistic assessment of risk.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: What warning does Caesar dismiss from the Soothsayer as he arrives at the Senate?
entries.answer: The earlier warning to beware the Ides of March, which Caesar dismisses since the day has arrived without apparent incident.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: What does Artemidorus attempt to do just before the assassination, and how does Caesar respond?
entries.answer: He attempts to hand Caesar a letter naming the conspirators and urges him to read it immediately, but Caesar sets the matter aside without reading it.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: What petition does Metellus Cimber bring before Caesar?
entries.answer: He petitions Caesar to allow his banished brother to return to Rome.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: How does Caesar respond to Metellus Cimber's petition, and what does his response reveal about his character?
entries.answer: He firmly refuses, comparing his own unwavering judgement to the fixed North Star, revealing his pride and confidence in his own unshakeable authority.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: Who draws Mark Antony away from Caesar just before the assassination, and why?
entries.answer: Trebonius, one of the conspirators, draws Antony away to ensure he cannot intervene or defend Caesar during the attack.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: Who strikes the first blow against Caesar?
entries.answer: Casca strikes the first blow.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: What causes Caesar to stop resisting his attackers?
entries.answer: Seeing that Brutus, whom he trusted and loved as a friend, is also among those stabbing him.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: Where does Caesar fall after being stabbed?
entries.answer: He falls dead at the foot of Pompey's statue.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: What does Cinna call out immediately after the assassination?
entries.answer: He calls out that liberty and freedom have been restored to Rome.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: What does Antony's servant ask on his behalf after the assassination?
entries.answer: He asks whether Antony may safely approach to mourn Caesar and whether he will be given a satisfactory explanation for why Caesar had to die.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: What permission does Brutus grant Antony, against Cassius's objection?
entries.answer: Brutus grants Antony permission to speak at Caesar's funeral, despite Cassius's warning that this could be dangerous to their cause.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: What does Antony reveal once left alone with Caesar's body?
entries.answer: He reveals, in a private aside, his genuine grief and fury beneath his outwardly composed manner toward the conspirators.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: Where does Brutus address the Roman citizens after Caesar's death?
entries.answer: He addresses them in the Forum, explaining that he acted for the good of Rome and not out of any personal hatred of Caesar.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: How does Antony's ironic repetition of "honourable men" work to persuade the crowd?
entries.answer: Repeatedly calling the conspirators "honourable men" while recounting Caesar's love for Rome and his generosity, he uses irony to make the crowd doubt whether the killing was truly honourable in any sense.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: What does Caesar's will provide for every Roman citizen, according to Antony?
entries.answer: Seventy-five drachmas, along with the use of his private walks, arbours and newly-planted orchards.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: How do the plebeians react once Antony reveals the contents of the will?
entries.answer: Overcome with grief and fury, they rush out determined to burn the houses of the conspirators to the ground.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: What happens to Brutus and Cassius after Antony's oration turns the crowd against them?
entries.answer: With their position destroyed by the mob's fury, they are forced to flee the city.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: Discuss how Shakespeare builds tension leading up to Caesar's assassination in this scene.
entries.answer:
Structured answer:

Introduction: Shakespeare carefully builds dramatic tension in the lead-up to the assassination through a sequence of ignored warnings and calculated staging by the conspirators.

Evidence: Caesar dismisses both the Soothsayer's earlier caution and Artemidorus's urgent letter naming the plotters, unknowingly walking past his last chances to avoid danger. The conspirators then use Metellus Cimber's petition as a pretext to draw physically close to Caesar, while Trebonius deliberately removes Mark Antony from the scene, ensuring no one can intervene once the attack begins.

Conclusion: This careful build-up, layering dramatic irony (the audience knowing what Caesar does not) with tense staging, makes the assassination, when it finally occurs, feel both inevitable and shocking.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: Explain the significance of Caesar's reaction upon seeing Brutus among his attackers.
entries.answer:
Structured answer:

Introduction: Caesar's response upon recognising Brutus among his assassins is the scene's most emotionally significant moment, shifting the assassination from purely political violence into personal tragedy.

Evidence: Though Caesar initially attempts to resist his attackers, he stops struggling entirely once he sees Brutus, a man he trusted and loved as a close friend, delivering his own blow, expressing his devastation in his famous final words before falling dead at the foot of Pompey's statue.

Conclusion: This moment underscores the play's deeper theme of betrayal, suggesting that the wound of broken trust and friendship affects Caesar even more profoundly than the physical violence itself.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: Analyse Brutus's decision to allow Mark Antony to speak at Caesar's funeral, and its dramatic significance.
entries.answer:
Structured answer:

Introduction: Brutus's decision to permit Mark Antony to speak at Caesar's funeral, made despite Cassius's explicit warning, is a pivotal moment whose consequences extend well beyond this scene.

Evidence: Brutus reassures Antony's servant that Antony will be safe and grants him permission to speak, trusting that a full explanation of the conspirators' motives will satisfy the Roman public. Cassius, more politically cautious, warns that Antony's rhetorical skill could turn public opinion against them, a warning Brutus dismisses.

Conclusion: This decision reveals Brutus's idealistic character — his belief in reason, fairness and open explanation — while also planting the dramatic seed for the political reversal that Antony's funeral oration will go on to cause.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: Discuss the theme of ambition and its dangers as presented in this scene from Julius Caesar.
entries.answer:
Structured answer:

Introduction: The theme of ambition and its dangers runs throughout the assassination scene, shaping both Caesar's own behaviour and the conspirators' justification for killing him.

Evidence: Caesar's proud refusal of Metellus Cimber's petition, in which he compares his own constancy to the fixed North Star among lesser stars, displays a confidence bordering on arrogance about his singular, unmatched authority. The conspirators, in turn, justify their assassination as a necessary defence of Roman liberty against precisely this kind of unchecked personal power, believing Caesar's ambition threatens to destroy the republic's traditions.

Conclusion: By presenting both Caesar's genuine confidence and the conspirators' genuine fear of tyranny, Shakespeare explores ambition as a complex, double-edged force — capable of building great achievement, but also of provoking violent resistance when it appears unchecked.

entries.unitTitle: Julius Caesar (Act III — The Assassination and the Funeral Orations)
entries.prompt: Analyse how Antony's funeral oration persuades the Roman crowd to turn against the conspirators.
entries.answer:
Structured answer:

Introduction: Antony's funeral oration is a masterclass in persuasive rhetoric, achieving through irony and emotional appeal what open accusation could never have achieved.

Evidence: Constrained by his promise not to blame the conspirators directly, Antony repeatedly labels them "honourable men" while piling up evidence of Caesar's love for the people, his victories and the inheritance his death has cost them — seventy-five drachmas and the use of his walks, arbours and newly-planted orchards for every citizen. Each repetition of "honourable" plants deeper doubt in the crowd's minds, until the label comes to mean the opposite of what it says. He ends by deliberately holding back, leaving the crowd to draw its own furious conclusions, which they do with devastating effect.

Conclusion: Antony's speech shows how carefully controlled tone, evidence and emotion can redirect the mood of an entire city, undoing Brutus's reasoned appeal and converting grief into fury against the conspirators.

entries.prompt: Part 1 — The motive: rivalry with Loona Bimberton
entries.answer: Mrs Packletide decides she must shoot a tiger, but her motive has nothing to do with courage or sport. It is driven almost entirely by her intense dislike of a fellow socialite, Loona Bimberton, who has recently been flown eleven miles by an Algerian aviator and has been dining out on the story ever since. Mrs Packletide reasons that only a personally procured tiger-skin, backed by a heavy harvest of press photographs, can successfully outshine that feat and restore her social standing. She has already mentally planned a lunch party at her house on Curzon Street, ostensibly in Loona's honour, with the tiger-skin as the centrepiece of conversation, and has designed in her mind the tiger-claw brooch she intends to gift Loona on her birthday. To make the hunt as safe and certain as possible, she offers one thousand rupees to any village that can arrange for her to shoot a tiger without much risk or exertion.
entries.notes: Establishes the satirical premise: vanity, not sportsmanship, drives the plot.

entries.prompt: Part 2 — The staged hunt
entries.answer: A neighbouring village obliges, offering the opportunity of an old, infirm tiger that has given up hunting large game and taken to killing the villagers' domestic animals instead. Mrs Packletide arrives with her paid companion, Louisa Mebbin, to witness and validate her triumph. A goat with a particularly persistent bleat is tethered as bait at a safe distance from Mrs Packletide's hiding place. When the tiger appears, Mrs Packletide fires — but it is Miss Mebbin who quietly points out that the bullet has actually struck the goat, not the tiger, and that the tiger itself appears to have collapsed and died, apparently of heart failure brought on by the shock of the gunshot noise, hastened by its own old age. Mrs Packletide is briefly annoyed at this discovery, but since she is nonetheless in possession of a dead tiger, and the villagers are eager for their promised thousand rupees, everyone quietly agrees to the fiction that she shot the beast herself.
entries.notes: The central comic irony: the "hunt" is entirely fraudulent.

entries.prompt: Part 3 — Manufactured fame
entries.answer: With the villagers complicit in the deception, Mrs Packletide faces the cameras with an easy conscience, and her photographs travel astonishingly far, appearing in newspapers as distant as an American paper and a Russian illustrated supplement. She hosts her planned lunch party in Loona Bimberton's honour with the tiger-skin displayed prominently, and follows through on gifting Loona the tiger-claw brooch, whose thank-you note Loona sends back in a tone of carefully repressed emotion — she pointedly declines the luncheon invitation itself. Mrs Packletide extends her triumph further by attending a fancy-dress ball dressed as Diana, the Greek goddess of the hunt, and the tiger-skin rug travels between London houses to be admired by county society. She only draws the line at Clovis's mischievous suggestion that she host a "primeval dance party" in which guests would wear the skins of animals they had personally slain.
entries.notes: Satirises high-society obsession with appearances and status.

entries.prompt: Part 4 — Blackmail and the price of the fraud
entries.answer: Some days later, Louisa Mebbin, the only witness to the truth of the hunt, quietly threatens to reveal that it was a goat, not Mrs Packletide's marksmanship, that was actually shot, and that the tiger had simply died of fright. To secure Miss Mebbin's permanent silence, Mrs Packletide is blackmailed into buying her a weekend cottage near Dorking for six hundred and eighty pounds. Miss Mebbin christens the cottage "Les Fauves" and plants its garden borders with tiger lilies, to the admiration of her friends, who wonder how she manages such a purchase on her modest means. Mrs Packletide, meanwhile, never again indulges in big-game shooting, remarking to curious friends only that "the incidental expenses are so heavy."
entries.notes: The story's final irony: the fraud costs Mrs Packletide far more than an honest hunt would have.

entries.prompt: Vanity and social one-upmanship
entries.answer: The entire plot is driven not by any genuine interest in hunting but by Mrs Packletide's desperate need to outdo her rival, Loona Bimberton, in the eyes of London society. Every action — offering rupees for a risk-free tiger, staging photographs, hosting a lunch party, gifting a brooch, attending a costume ball as Diana — is calculated purely for social effect rather than for any authentic achievement. Saki satirises a social world in which reputation is built entirely on appearances and performance rather than substance, showing how far a wealthy woman will go, and how much she will spend and risk being exposed, merely to seem impressive to a rival she dislikes.

entries.prompt: Irony and the gap between appearance and reality
entries.answer: Saki constructs the story around a series of ironies: the "brave huntress" actually shoots a goat by mistake; the tiger dies of fright rather than any bullet; the villagers who should be honest instead collude in a lie for money; and Mrs Packletide's triumphant public image is entirely built on a private falsehood only she and Miss Mebbin know. The persistent gap between how things appear (a triumphant hunt) and how they actually are (a farce) is the story's comic engine, and it exposes the emptiness of the fame and admiration Mrs Packletide receives.

entries.prompt: The corrupting power of money and the vulnerability it creates
entries.answer: Money drives every relationship in the story: Mrs Packletide uses it to buy a "safe" tiger hunt from the village, and the villagers accept it readily enough to lie on her behalf. But money also becomes the very thing that traps her, since her wealth and desire to protect her reputation make her permanently vulnerable to blackmail once Miss Mebbin discovers the truth. Saki suggests that a fortune spent buying a false reputation ultimately buys very little real security, since the truth remains in someone else's hands, ready to be leveraged at any time.

entries.prompt: Blackmail and quiet exploitation between social unequals
entries.answer: Louisa Mebbin, though nominally Mrs Packletide's "paid companion" and social inferior, ends the story in the stronger position, extracting a substantial cottage from her employer simply by holding the truth over her. This role reversal satirises how dependence on appearances can invert real power: the person with the most damaging information, however socially modest, can dominate the person with the most wealth and status. Miss Mebbin's calm, businesslike manner in delivering her threat — never raising her voice, simply mentioning the cottage "with seeming irrelevance" — makes the exploitation all the more pointed and comic.

entries.prompt: Mrs Packletide
entries.answer: Mrs Packletide is a wealthy, socially ambitious Englishwoman whose actions throughout the story are governed almost entirely by her rivalry with Loona Bimberton rather than by any genuine love of adventure or hunting. She is willing to spend a thousand rupees to guarantee a risk-free tiger kill purely for the social capital it will bring her, and she happily accepts the villagers' fiction that she shot the tiger once she realises the truth is embarrassing. Her vanity is further shown in her elaborate plans for a lunch party, a gifted brooch, and a costume-ball appearance as the huntress-goddess Diana. Ultimately she is revealed as shallow and easily manipulated, paying a huge price in blackmail to protect an image built on nothing.

entries.prompt: Loona Bimberton
entries.answer: Loona Bimberton never appears in a hunting scene herself, but her recent flight of eleven miles with an Algerian aviator is the spark that sets the entire plot in motion, since Mrs Packletide cannot bear to be socially outdone by her. Loona's reaction to Mrs Packletide's manufactured triumph — refusing to look at illustrated papers for weeks, sending an icily restrained thank-you note for the tiger-claw brooch, and declining the luncheon invitation outright — reveals that she recognises she has been beaten in their unspoken rivalry and resents it deeply, even while maintaining polite appearances herself.

entries.prompt: Louisa Mebbin
entries.answer: Louisa Mebbin is Mrs Packletide's paid companion, present at the hunt ostensibly to serve as a witness to her employer's bravery. She is the only person who realises, and states plainly, that Mrs Packletide actually shot the goat and that the tiger died of fright — a moment of blunt honesty that briefly threatens the entire fiction. Later, however, Miss Mebbin proves herself calculating and quietly ruthless, using her knowledge of the truth to blackmail Mrs Packletide into buying her an expensive weekend cottage. Her cool, understated manner of extracting this reward, and her decision to decorate the cottage garden with tiger lilies, gives the story much of its dry comic irony.

entries.prompt: Clovis
entries.answer: Clovis is a minor character who appears briefly during Mrs Packletide's social triumph, suggesting — half in jest — that she should host a "primeval dance party" in which every guest wears the skin of an animal they have personally killed. Mrs Packletide, despite embracing every other opportunity to display her supposed hunting feat, draws the line at this suggestion, which highlights the limits of even her vanity and adds a further touch of Saki's characteristic satirical wit to the story's high-society setting.

entries.prompt: What does the story teach about the dangers of vanity and jealousy?
entries.answer: The story shows that allowing jealousy and the desire to impress others to govern one's decisions can lead a person into deception, expense and eventual humiliation. Evidence: Mrs Packletide's entire elaborate scheme — offering a thousand rupees, staging photographs, hosting parties — exists solely to outdo Loona Bimberton, and it ultimately costs her far more, in money and vulnerability to blackmail, than any honest pursuit would have. The lesson is that chasing status through appearances rather than genuine achievement leaves a person exposed and dependent on others' silence.

entries.prompt: What does the story teach about honesty and the consequences of deception?
entries.answer: Saki demonstrates that a lie, however successfully it is initially covered up, tends to leave the liar permanently vulnerable to whoever else knows the truth. Evidence: Mrs Packletide's fabricated hunting triumph is safe from public exposure only as long as Louisa Mebbin chooses to stay silent, and Miss Mebbin eventually exploits that silence for a costly cottage. The lesson is that dishonesty, even when it appears to succeed, creates lasting risk rather than genuine security.

entries.answer: She wanted to outdo her rival Loona Bimberton, who had recently been flown eleven miles by an Algerian aviator and had been enjoying the resulting attention.

entries.answer: She offered one thousand rupees for the opportunity to shoot a tiger without much risk or exertion.

entries.answer: An old, infirm tiger that had given up hunting large game because of its age and had taken to killing villagers' domestic animals instead.

entries.answer: She actually shot the goat that had been tethered as bait; the tiger itself died separately, apparently of heart failure from the noise.
